questions.question: Jay Bhattacharya of Stanford, Martin Kulldorff of Harvard and Sunetra Gupta of Oxford, three professors who study health and disease, signed the Great Barrington Declaration on 4 October 2020, seven months into the COVID-19 pandemic. What did their declaration propose?
questions.answer: Shield the old and frail, and let the young and healthy live normally
choices: Shield the old and frail, and let the young and healthy live normally
Let all ages live normally, so the virus would spread and burn out sooner
Keep schools shut, but open shops, offices and restaurants again
Test everyone every week, and isolate all who test positive
questions.context: The authors called it 'Focused Protection': 'Those who are not vulnerable should immediately be allowed to resume life as normal', and 'Schools and universities should be open for in-person teaching', while nursing homes used staff with acquired immunity and retired people had groceries delivered. Critics answered in The Lancet that month that keeping large parts of the population apart for long was 'practically impossible', and that spread among the young would reach the whole population. The plan was never to let the virus run through every age alike.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks students to state a claim fairly, in its own words, before judging it, and the declaration is a case where the plan was often described as something it did not say.

questions.question: Francis Collins, director of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), judged the Great Barrington Declaration dangerous, as did the scientists who warned in The Lancet that spread among the young would reach the whole population. On 8 October 2020 he wrote to Anthony Fauci about its 'three fringe epidemiologists'. The email became public in December 2021 through a public-records request. What did it call for?
questions.answer: A quick and devastating published take down of its premises
choices: A quick and devastating published take down of its premises
A public debate between its authors and the agency's experts
A formal complaint to the universities that employed its authors
A small trial of its plan before any national decision
questions.context: Fauci answered the same night with an article from Wired that he said 'debunks' the declaration. Collins, who later said he had been 'deeply worried' and believed the plan would cost lives, called its three authors 'very distinguished' and said in 2023, 'I regret that I used some terminology that I probably shouldn't', while holding that the plan had been dangerous. The emails were released to the American Institute for Economic Research, which had hosted the declaration's signing.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that scientific claims are settled by evidence and open, sceptical review, and this email is a documented case of how one dissenting claim was met.

questions.question: Sweden kept its preschools and schools open for children under 16 through the spring of 2020, with no mask rules in the classrooms. Jonas Ludvigsson and his colleagues searched the national health records for every one of the country's 1.95 million children aged 1 to 16, from March to June. What did they report in January 2021?
questions.answer: None died of COVID-19, and 15 needed intensive care
choices: None died of COVID-19, and 15 needed intensive care
None died of COVID-19, but over 1,500 needed intensive care
About 40 died of COVID-19, most of them already ill
About 400 died of COVID-19, most of them under five
questions.context: No child with COVID-19 died, and 15 were treated in intensive care for it or a related inflammatory illness, about one child in 130,000; 4 of them already had other illnesses. Deaths from all causes, 69, were close to the 65 of the four months before. The study counted serious illness only: it did not measure whether children carried the virus home to adults.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science teaches students to judge a claim by measured data, and national records gave a complete count of a whole age group rather than a sample.

questions.question: Anna Eva Hallin and her colleagues compared the reading tests of 97,073 Swedish pupils in grades 1 to 3, from before and during the pandemic, while Sweden's primary schools stayed open. In the Netherlands, where schools shut for eight weeks in 2020, Per Engzell's team had measured a loss of about a fifth of a school year. What did the Swedish team find?
questions.answer: Reading was no worse during the pandemic than before
choices: Reading was no worse during the pandemic than before
Reading fell by about a fifth of a year, as in the Netherlands
Reading held up, except among pupils from poorer homes
Reading fell, but only among the youngest, in grade 1
questions.context: Word reading and understanding were no lower than before, the share of weak readers did not grow, and pupils from poorer homes were not hit harder, so the authors concluded that open schools had served Sweden's young pupils well. In the Netherlands the loss had been up to 60 percent larger among pupils from less-educated homes. Open doors did not mean no disruption: Swedish 4th-graders read less well in an international study of 2021 than in 2016, a fall Sweden's schools agency laid partly on the pandemic: sickness absence and short closures had disrupted teaching for two months or more in about one school in three.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn to judge an outcome against a comparison group, and pupils in open Swedish schools are the natural comparison for pupils whose schools closed.

questions.question: The National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), a test given to samples of American pupils, showed in 2022 the largest falls in maths scores at grades 4 and 8 since its maths test began in 1990. Thomas Kane of Harvard and Sean Reardon of Stanford matched local test results to how long each school district had taught remotely in 2020-21. What did they report?
questions.answer: Districts kept remote longer lost more; in-person ones lost too
choices: Districts kept remote longer lost more; in-person ones lost too
Only districts kept remote lost ground; in-person ones held steady
Districts kept remote longer lost no more than in-person ones
Districts kept remote longer lost less, as parents helped at home
questions.context: Losses were greater where districts stayed online longer, though many districts back in person lost ground too, and the poorest quarter of schools lost about two-thirds of a year in maths. The researchers warned that they could not fully separate remote schooling from other ways those districts differed, and Kane said remote learning was not the only thing driving the losses. A study he co-wrote in May 2022 had called remote instruction 'a primary driver' of the widening gaps between rich and poor schools.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade investigation design teaches confounding variables, and the districts that stayed remote longer differed from the others in more than their schooling.

questions.question: Tom Jefferson and his colleagues pooled randomised trials for a Cochrane review in January 2023 and concluded that wearing masks in the community 'probably makes little or no difference' to flu-like or COVID-like illness. In March, Karla Soares-Weiser, Cochrane's editor-in-chief, called the reading 'masks don't work' inaccurate and misleading. What did she say the trials had really tested?
questions.answer: Whether urging people to wear masks slowed the spread
choices: Whether urging people to wear masks slowed the spread
Whether laws ordering people into masks slowed the spread
Whether a mask protects the one person who wears it
Whether masks block droplets when tested on a dummy head
questions.context: The trials compared groups offered masks and encouraged to wear them with groups that were not, and many did not wear them: in the largest, 42.3 percent of the mask group wore one, against 13.3 percent of the others. Such a trial measures what urging masks achieves among real people, not what a mask does on a face that wears it; Soares-Weiser called the results 'inconclusive', and said the review could not answer whether wearing a mask itself lowers a person's risk. The review's authors wrote that the low adherence 'hampers drawing firm conclusions', and that large, well-designed trials were still needed.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks what a study's design can and cannot show, and a trial of offering masks is a different test from a trial of wearing them.

questions.question: Scientists writing in The Lancet in October 2020, when COVID-19 was less than a year old, said there was 'no evidence for lasting protective immunity' after infection. The COVID-19 Forecasting Team pooled 65 studies from 19 countries in The Lancet in 2023 to measure how well a past infection protected people over the months that followed. How did that protection stand 40 weeks on?
questions.answer: Strong against severe illness, though weaker against catching it again
choices: Strong against severe illness, though weaker against catching it again
Strong against catching it again, though weaker against severe illness
Strong against both, with no fall at all through the months
Gone against both, after a few months of strong protection
questions.context: At 40 weeks, protection against severe illness was still 88.9 to 90.2 percent for every form of the virus studied, while protection against catching the newest form again had fallen to 36.1 percent. Thucydides saw the same pattern in the plague of Athens in 430 BC: those who had recovered nursed the sick without fear, 'for the same man was never attacked twice—never at least fatally.' In 2020 too little time had passed to measure lasting protection; by 2023 there were years of data.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that a claim made on little data is revised as evidence accumulates, and here two measured kinds of protection behaved differently over time.

questions.question: Jonas Herby, Lars Jonung and Steve Hanke, three economists, pooled the studies that measured COVID-19 deaths under the lockdowns of spring 2020 in Europe and the United States. Their working paper of January 2022 put the cut in deaths at 0.2 percent; their revised version, which became a book in 2023, put it at 3.2 percent. What did those percentages compare?
questions.answer: Deaths under strict rules with deaths under lighter ones
choices: Deaths under strict rules with deaths under lighter ones
Deaths under strict rules with deaths under no rules at all
Deaths counted in 2020 with deaths that models had forecast
Deaths from COVID-19 with deaths caused by the rules
questions.context: The figures set stricter, legally required rules against lighter, more voluntary ones such as Sweden's, not against doing nothing, and the authors gave people's own voluntary caution 'a significant role' in the fall in deaths. Critics such as Seth Flaxman of Oxford objected that the review left out every study built on the science of how disease spreads, and Samir Bhatt of Imperial College that it counted even a single rule, such as a mask order, as a lockdown. The economist David Paton answered that leaving out modelling studies was 'not controversial'.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks what a comparison group is, and a percentage cut means little until its baseline is known.

questions.question: Twenty-seven public-health scientists condemned 'conspiracy theories suggesting that COVID-19 does not have a natural origin' in The Lancet in February 2020, when about three in four new human diseases were known to come from animals. The FBI later judged a laboratory accident the likelier origin, as its director said in February 2023, and the US Department of Energy's view, reported that month, was the same. What did the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) conclude in January 2025?
questions.answer: A lab accident was likelier, held with low confidence
choices: A lab accident was likelier, held with low confidence
A lab accident was likelier, held with high confidence
A jump from animals was likelier, held with low confidence
A jump from animals was likelier, held with high confidence
questions.context: The CIA judged a research-related origin more likely but said, 'We have low confidence in this judgement', and that both a laboratory and a natural origin 'remain plausible'; it had looked again at existing intelligence, not new evidence. The FBI held its judgement with moderate confidence and the Energy Department with low, while four other US agencies and the National Intelligence Council still leaned, with low confidence, toward a jump from animals. The question is not settled: in a 2024 survey of 168 experts the average estimate was 77 percent for a natural origin.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn to separate a conclusion from the confidence it is held with, and to call an open question open.

questions.question: Jay Bhattacharya, a Stanford professor of medicine and one of the three authors of the Great Barrington Declaration, was nominated in November 2024 to head a federal body. The US Senate confirmed him on 25 March 2025, and he took office on 1 April. Which body did he then lead?
choices: The National Institutes of Health
The Food and Drug Administration
The National Science Foundation
The Department of Health and Human Services
questions.context: He became the 18th director of the National Institutes of Health, the main US government agency for medical research, with a budget of about 47 billion dollars in 2024; it was the agency Francis Collins had led when he wrote his email of October 2020. In February 2026 Bhattacharya was also made acting head of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science covers the institutions that fund and review research, and the NIH is the main US government body for medical research.
